Molten Sea
MOHL-ten SEE
n. (the great brasen laver of Solomon's temple)
Hebrew yam mutsaq, a cast or molten sea, from yam, a sea, and yatsaq, to pour out or cast metal; called also the brasen sea and the sea of brass. Named as the molten sea twice.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The molten sea was the enormous cast-brass basin that stood in the court of Solomon's temple, holding the water for the priests' washing: “And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about” (1 Kings 7:23). It rested on twelve brasen oxen, three facing each quarter, and was ornamented beneath the brim with knops and lily work. It is called a sea because of its size; the tabernacle's laver had been a vessel a man could carry, and this held, by the account in Kings, two thousand baths. The thing it supplied was washing. Blood was dealt with at the altar; water was dealt with here, and no priest went into the holy place with unwashed hands and feet. The two together give the whole of the believer's standing — the altar for guilt and the sea for defilement, justification and sanctification in brass and water, and neither one optional for a man who meant to serve. The Chaldeans broke it up: “the brasen sea that was in the house of the LORD, did the Chaldees break in pieces, and carried the brass of them to Babylon” (2 Kings 25:13). In the Revelation the sea before the throne is no longer for washing but is of glass, clear as crystal, because in that house the washing is finished.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Molten sea, the great basin of cast brass in the court of Solomon's temple, ten cubits across and five high, resting on twelve brasen oxen, holding water for the priests' washing.

Hebrew yam mutsaq, a molten or cast sea, from yam, a sea, and yatsaq, to pour or cast.

Ten cubits from brim to brim, five cubits high, thirty cubits about, 1 Kings 7:23.

Resting upon twelve brasen oxen, three toward each quarter, 1 Kings 7:25.

Called also the brasen sea and the sea, 2 Kings 25:13.

Answering to the laver of the tabernacle, but far greater, Exodus 30:18.

Key Scripture

1Ki 7:23 — "And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about."

2Ch 4:2 — "Also he made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in compass, and five cubits the height thereof; and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about."

2Ki 25:13 — "And the pillars of brass that were in the house of the LORD, and the bases, and the brasen sea that was in the house of the LORD, did the Chaldees break in pieces, and carried the brass of them to Babylon."

Jer 52:17 — "Also the pillars of brass that were in the house of the LORD, and the bases, and the brasen sea that was in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans brake, and carried all the brass of them to Babylon."

Modern Corruption

The sanctuary's washing is collapsed into its sacrifice, as though cleansing were nothing once guilt is answered; Scripture sets the altar and the sea in the same court.

expand to see more

The antinomian error treats the altar as having made the sea unnecessary — guilt answered, therefore defilement indifferent, and holiness an optional refinement for the earnest. The architecture of the court refutes it. Both stood there, and the priest who passed the altar and skipped the sea did not enter the holy place. Justification and sanctification are distinct and inseparable: the first is a verdict and the second a work, and the same Christ who is the propitiation is also the one who washes His church with water by the word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the washing is for those already belonging to the house. Only priests used the sea; it was not for the nations outside but for men already consecrated, who yet got dirty doing holy work. That is the Christian life. The sea of glass in Revelation 4 is the end of it, standing clear and still before the throne because there is nothing left to wash off, and the twelve oxen that bore the water have become a multitude that no man can number.
